subject: Comments on three issues before the Commission
comment: Dear Ms. Milliken and Members of the Commission: Please accept the following comments regarding issues before you. 1. Pickleball‐please accept this comment regarding the conditional use application for the conversion of a concrete “patio” located at 1961 Venus Court, Park Meadows to a pickleball court. The applicant has cited the idea that private pickleball courts contribute to the notion of building community. Access to private pickleball courts is generally limited to family, friends, and invited participants‐such courts are rarely open to neighborhood or public use. As such it is not unreasonable to find such private facilities akin to gated communities‐only owners and invited others are welcome. All others are purposely excluded. This does not seem to be community building. Community building has been less than evident of late in regard to this particular conditional use application in that one of the adult sons (over 18) of the owner of 1961 Venus Court, has taken to saluting us with his middle finger whenever he may encounter us outside on our property or walking on the public streets and sidewalks in our neighborhood. If this is the kind of community building engendered with private pickleball courts and their many concomitant issues, perhaps such courts should not be approved as evidently they do not build community. 2. Building moratorium‐a positive idea in the midst of what some describe as explosive growth in our community. Slowing things down is always a good idea as it provides time for information gathering, study, reflection, input, planning and, finally, decision making. A year or longer moratorium should not be an issue, 1 577 particularly as extant approvals granted over 30 or 40 years ago have not been exercised in a timely manner. Perhaps a focus of work during such a moratorium should be on legislating a seven year sunset provision on all growth approvals/permits. If no shovel is in the ground within seven years, a reasonable timeline to secure plans and financial support, a project must start the entire approval process again. 3. PEG proposal for the parking lots at the Resort‐see the preceding comment. I have lived in Park City for 40 years. I am aghast at the proposed PEG development. I urge the Planning Commission to visit Sugarhouse in SLC, specifically the southwest corner of Eleventh East and 21st South. This is what 90 feet of high density housing looks and, perhaps more importantly, feels like. Whilst there, take a stroll through the walks‐ in, around and through these projects. Try to see and feel like residents of Old Town in PC will see and feel, what veteran residents of Park City will see and feel. The proposed PEG project is not a beginning but it may well be the end of the community we know and love. Thank you for reading. Sincerely, Brian Schiller P.O. In many respects the Commissioners’ response to the Staff Report was very encouraging (in that they demonstrated a constructive understanding of the sensitive issues presented). comment: As stated prior to my comments this evening, I have the utmost respect for our Planning Commission and appreciate their service to our community. My comments in no way are meant to be a criticism to any of the commissioners. As the City Manager has oversight/authority over the Planning Department and he along with the City Council have oversight of the Planning Commission, I’m bringing these comments to you. With regards to Planning Commission meeting protocol, I’m assuming applicants are given deadlines for their submissions to allow appropriate time for the Planning Department to review and publish a comprehensive report. What is the mechanism for enforcement of these deadlines? I believe it reasonable that a failure to meet a deadline should mean automatic continuance until the next month. The Planning Staff generally have more than one application on their desk and I think they would find it beneficial as well. The Commissioners would also benefit as agenda items lacking a comprehensive report in the packet for them to review ahead of time, would be continued. Contrary to what the Planning Director stated last night, this has happened on more than one occasion. Please consider providing additional guidance to the Planning Director and Staff that it is not the City’s responsibility to make an application work and gain approval per the LMC. The City does not have to come up with solutions and work arounds for any application. It is the applicant’s responsibility or burden of proof to come up with those solutions and present them in a cohesive, comprehensive manner for a timely and thorough review. Commissioners often ask for additional or new information during the review of an application and never receive it. The use of a checklist by the Planning Department to reference as to whether that information is ever received would be a helpful tool for both planning staff in preparation and the applicant in making sure they’ve met their burden of proof. Again, it is actually the applicant’s responsibility to meet the burden of proof. If the applicant chooses not to provide that information, then it gets noted as such on this checklist and prior to any public hearing or action, this checklist is published with the packet. In case an example is needed, in December, a commissioner asked for car counts at an intersection. The applicant said no and if the commission wanted that data, they could ask the city to get it. This response would get noted and would only change if the applicant subsequently changed their mind and provided the information. Applicants often bring new information to the meetings in the form of exhibits or otherwise. This information consequently isn’t available ahead of time for review by the Commission or public. Is it worth considering having applicants provide a copy of all presented materials to be included in the next packet along with the Public Input for purposes of reference later on? There have been multiple instances where an applicant is asked a question and their response is they’ve provided the answer previously and then re-iterate what they believe to be the answer, which may or may not actually be correct. If the presented information is provided on screen only, it’s very difficult to go back to that audio at a later date and find it. Having access to a “hard copy” would seemingly be beneficial to both the Commission and the public and perhaps make meetings more efficient. I raised this during last night’s Planning meeting and the discussion by the Commissioner’s following indicated they would very much like this change to happen effective with last night’s meeting and collected for previous meetings. I respectfully request a follow up to make sure this actually happens. Requests were made of planning staff over the last 18 months for this and it has not happened. With the commissioners agreeing it should, I’m hopeful, but not convinced our Planning Director will implement it without additional encouragement to do so. During the Planning Commission meetings, the Chat function is disabled. I’ll admit some months ago, a meeting occurred where it had not been disabled and when an applicant made an inaccurate or inconsistent statement, the public made note of it via the chat function. There were no obscenities. Within a few minutes, the Chat was disabled and has been ever since. In addition, the meeting is held in a manner that we cannot see who else or how many are attending. Zoom has this capability and if we were meeting in person, we’d know who else and how many others were there. Please consider making both of these adjustments going forward as long as a Zoom option is offered. Finally, I attend most planning meetings and play them back if I have a conflict. I also have the planning meeting schedule on my calendar. Snow Park DV is typically the 2nd Wednesday of the month and PCMR is the 3rd Wednesday of the month. For PCMR, since November 2020 every single meeting has been scheduled for the 3rd Wednesday. Crazy, but I and others in the community actually make plans around this schedule. In January, the Planning Commission requested we get back to two meetings a month and shorten the meetings. The Snow Park meeting for February still went until 10:30pm and was on the 2nd Wednesday. The PCMR meeting adjourned at 9:00pm in spite of the applicant going 23 minutes over their allotted time and was held on the 3rd Wednesday (last night). Now, a public hearing – perhaps the very last time for the public to weigh in on the PCMR project, has been scheduled for the 4th Wednesday of March. This project has been under review for almost two years with no end in sight. This is a change in the schedule at the most inopportune time for the public. I humbly request direction be given to the Planning Department by the appropriate authority to hold the public hearing on the 3rd Wednesday of March and remain consistent with the last 16 months scheduling. Thank you again for the opportunity to speak. I 100% agree there is a different vibe with this Council and am excited about our City's future under your governance.

comment: We can sum up the last couple of weeks by one word: REACTIVE. Traffic around the base has been an issue for more than just this season. However, as Councilor Gerber pointed out in early January, this year it seems worse. What did Vail Resorts do about it? Nothing. Two weeks ago, Councilor Gerber asked if anything had been done in preparation for the President’s Day weekend with regards to traffic. In addition, over two dozen citizens gathered either online or in person at that same meeting to raise concerns. What did VR do about it? Made a bunch of changes to parking and circulation with very little consistent communication. It was a mess. The problem is this is all reactive. Did PCMR really not know what was going on until two weeks ago? As KPCW interviewed a City representative and Mike Lewis this morning, it was pointed out some changes could have been implemented before this season even started. Ideas that others have suggested for over a year to Vail/PEG with regards to possible improvements or strategies now were included in the interview. Mr. Lewis basically replied it was too heavy a lift for this season, they’d continue to do what they can and maybe next season they could try some of these other things. He’s right. It’s too late to be pro-active now for this season, we’re in the thick of it. But I’m reasonably confident, if we don’t stay on them like glue, once this ski season is over, there will be little to no action in preparation for next season and it’ll be the same situation just a season later. I urge the City to do what they can to hold Vail accountable and insist on a new word moving forward with regards to resort parking and traffic: PROACTIVE. Comments by Council were spot on and hopefully will result in solutions and improvements by PCMR.

comment: I wasn't able to submit a comment for the presentation by Vail Resorts. I haven't seen the lines match the wait times more than a few times in my 40 (short) days on the mountain. How can you say the data is good? Not one of my friends, neighbors or colleagues have seen anything different. Doesn't seem like a solid argument at all. Not to mention the new line forecast system that doesn't work. It just doesn't add up. Additionally, I have worked on systems that counted guests entering and exciting different venues in the past and they were not that difficult to configure. This was 8+ years ago so I'm sure the technology has improved. Also, if the conversion of day passes to epic pass products was 1:1 then share the data because it's REALLY hard to believe. I do not want to see Vail fail. I want to see you succeed, but your product and experience has been an order of magnitude worse this year than any previous year that I, or anyone I have spoken with, has ever experienced. This is not a Park City only problem, but a Vail problem. https://instagram.com/epicliftlines
